questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Charge and current are different quantities
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a quantity of charge from a rate of flow of charge
questions.stem: A battery drives charge steadily round a closed circuit, and an ammeter in one wire reads a constant 2.0 A. Which statement correctly separates the two quantities involved?

options.text: Current is the rate at which charge passes a point, and charge is the amount itself
Charge is the rate of flow and current is the amount stored in the wire
options.misconception: swaps the two quantities, treating charge as a rate and current as a stored amount

options.text: Current is the amount of charge held in the battery at any one instant
options.misconception: confuses a stored amount of charge with a flow rate

options.text: Charge and current are two names for one quantity in different units
options.misconception: believes the two names are interchangeable because both appear in the circuit

questions.explanation: Charge is measured in coulombs and says how much of it there is; current is measured in amperes and says how much of it passes each second, so 2.0 A means 2.0 C every second. The tempting swap fails because a rate cannot be stored anywhere in the circuit: the charge in the battery does not rise and fall with the reading. Treating current as a stored amount also fails dimensionally, since amperes per second would be a rate of rates, which no circuit has.
questions.hint: Ask what the reading would be if the same charge went past twice as fast.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: A battery as a potential difference
questions.learningObjective: state that a cell maintains a potential difference across its terminals
questions.stem: A student says a battery holds charge and supplies current. Which statement is the correct one about what a working cell maintains between its two terminals?

options.text: A potential difference, which is what drives the current round the outside circuit
A current, which is pushed into the wires the moment the circuit is closed
options.misconception: believes the cell delivers a current rather than a voltage

options.text: A steady ammeter reading, which stays the same however the load is changed
options.misconception: believes the current is fixed and the voltage has to give way instead

options.text: A resistance, which sets how much current the terminals will let through
options.misconception: confuses the internal resistance with the driving voltage

questions.explanation: A cell does chemical work against its own internal resistance and keeps its two terminals at a fixed difference in potential, and that difference is what pushes charge round the external circuit. The current is not fixed: a cell can supply more current when a lower-resistance load is connected, which is why the ammeter reading changes with the load while the terminal voltage stays close to the emf. Describing the cell as setting a resistance confuses the internal resistance with the emf, which are separate quantities with different units.
questions.hint: A cell is rated in volts, not in amperes, and think about what happens when you load it.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: The junction rule as conservation of charge
questions.learningObjective: state which conservation principle Kirchhoff's junction rule expresses
questions.stem: Kirchhoff's junction rule is applied where three wires meet at one node. Which conservation principle does that rule express?

options.text: Conservation of charge, so charge arriving at the node must leave it
Conservation of energy, so power arriving at the node must leave it
options.misconception: picks energy conservation, which is the loop rule rather than the junction rule

options.text: Conservation of momentum, so the forces on the three wires must balance
options.misconception: picks momentum conservation, which says nothing about a lumped node

options.text: Conservation of mass, so no material may leave the junction at all
options.misconception: picks mass conservation and reads it as forbidding outflow

questions.explanation: Nothing can pile up at a node, so in any interval the charge going in equals the charge coming out, and that is exactly what the junction rule states. The tempting answer, energy, is the job of the other rule: the loop rule conserves energy around a closed path because the work done climbing a potential difference is recovered coming down. Momentum and mass play no part in a lumped circuit node, where charges arrive and leave without any need to be balanced in pairs.
questions.hint: Ask what would physically happen if charge did arrive faster than it left.

questions.topic: Balance condition in a bridge network
questions.learningObjective: state the condition under which the detector in a bridge network reads zero
questions.stem: A four-resistor bridge has a sensitive current detector in the branch that joins the two midpoints. What must be true of the network for that detector to read zero?

options.text: The two arm ratios are equal, so both midpoints sit at the same potential
The two midpoints sit at different potentials, so the two drops cancel
options.misconception: reads a null reading as the two midpoint potentials being different

options.text: All four arms are equal, so the two branches carry identical currents
options.misconception: believes equal arms are required when equal ratios are what matter

options.text: The detector branch is removed, so no current can flow through it
options.misconception: produces a null by deleting the branch rather than by balancing it

questions.explanation: No current flows through the detector when the two nodes it joins are at one and the same potential, and that happens when the ratio of the two arms on one side equals the ratio on the other, however unequal the individual arms are. The all-equal answer is a sufficient condition and nothing more: a 600, 900, 400 arm set balances against 600 ohms on the fourth corner, with three different values. Removing the branch avoids the reading but destroys the measurement, which is the whole point of the circuit.
questions.hint: Compare the potential at each midpoint as a fraction of the supply, not the currents.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Turning a galvanometer into an ammeter
questions.learningObjective: explain how a low-resistance shunt converts a galvanometer into an ammeter
questions.stem: A bare galvanometer deflects full scale when 0.50 mA passes through it, and its movement must not carry more than that. How is it adapted to read much larger currents?

options.text: A low-resistance shunt is connected across it so most current bypasses the movement
A high-resistance shunt is connected in series so it limits the current
options.misconception: puts a series resistance where a bypass is needed, so the meter reads far too little

options.text: A low-resistance shunt is connected in series so it drops the excess voltage
options.misconception: adds resistance in the current path instead of shunting the movement

options.text: The movement is replaced by a coil of many turns to raise its current capacity
options.misconception: believes more turns let more current through the same movement

questions.explanation: The galvanometer tolerates only 0.50 mA, so the extra current has to go somewhere else, and a low-resistance path across the movement takes the excess while the movement keeps its share and its full-scale reading. Putting resistance in series does the opposite: it reduces the current through the movement, so the scale would be wrong. More turns raises the resistance of the movement, which lowers the current through it for a given voltage, so it cannot raise the current capacity.
questions.hint: Ask where the excess current has to go, and which arrangement lets it go.

questions.topic: Where an ammeter goes
questions.learningObjective: place an ammeter so that it reads branch current without changing the circuit
questions.stem: An ammeter is built with a resistance as close to zero as it can be made. Given that design, where must it be connected to read the current through a lamp, and what does it do to the circuit?

options.text: In series with the lamp, so the circuit resistance is that of the lamp alone
In parallel with the lamp, so the circuit resistance is that of the lamp alone
options.misconception: puts the meter across the component instead of in the current path

options.text: In series with the lamp, so the circuit resistance is raised slightly
options.misconception: believes the meter must add resistance even though it is built near zero

options.text: In parallel with the lamp, so the circuit resistance is raised slightly
options.misconception: combines the wrong placement with a claim that the meter adds resistance

questions.explanation: To read the current that flows through a lamp, the meter has to carry that same current, which means being in line with it, in series. Because the ammeter is built with almost no resistance, dropping it in series leaves the total resistance, and therefore the lamp current, essentially unchanged. Across the lamp it would be a different story: a near-zero resistance in parallel is a short circuit, not a measurement.
questions.hint: The meter must carry the current it is reporting, so follow the path of that current.

questions.topic: Where a voltmeter goes
questions.learningObjective: place a voltmeter so that it reads a potential difference without drawing current
questions.stem: A voltmeter is built with a resistance as close to infinite as it can be made. Given that design, where must it be connected to read the potential difference across a lamp, and what does it do to the circuit?

options.text: In parallel across the lamp, drawing so little current the lamp is unaffected
In series with the lamp, drawing so little current the lamp is unaffected
options.misconception: puts the meter in the current path, where its high resistance blocks the current

options.text: In parallel across the lamp, drawing a large current that dims the lamp
options.misconception: claims a near-infinite resistance still draws a heavy current

options.text: In series with the lamp, drawing a large current that dims the lamp
options.misconception: combines the wrong placement with a claim of heavy current draw

questions.explanation: A potential difference exists between two points, so the voltmeter must span those points, in parallel with the component whose voltage is wanted. Its near-infinite resistance means almost no current is taken, so the circuit keeps working as before and the reading is the true voltage. In series the same high resistance would leave nothing for the lamp: the meter would take nearly the whole supply and the lamp would go dark.
questions.hint: A voltmeter compares two points, so ask which two points it has to touch.

questions.topic: Ammeter wrongly placed in parallel
questions.learningObjective: predict the effect of connecting an ammeter across a source
questions.stem: A student breaks a lamp circuit and connects the ammeter across the two terminals of the battery instead of in line with the lamp. What happens inside the circuit?

options.text: It shorts the battery, so a very large current flows through the ammeter
It opens the circuit, so no current flows anywhere in the battery
options.misconception: treats the ammeter as if it had the high resistance of a voltmeter

options.text: It reads the battery voltage correctly and nothing else in the circuit changes
options.misconception: believes the meter changes what it measures and not what it measures

options.text: The lamp still lights, because the ammeter carries the current instead of it
options.misconception: believes a parallel route diverts current without removing the lamp's own

questions.explanation: The ammeter is a near-zero resistance, and a near-zero resistance placed directly across the terminals is the definition of a short circuit, so the current is limited only by the battery's own internal resistance and can be large enough to damage it. Treating the ammeter as a high resistance gets the two instruments the wrong way round. The lamp going out is not diversion, because the lamp and the ammeter are in parallel, so the low-resistance path simply takes the voltage for itself.
questions.hint: Ask what a resistance of almost zero, connected across a battery, is called.

questions.topic: Voltmeter wrongly placed in series
questions.learningObjective: predict the effect of connecting a voltmeter in series with a component
questions.stem: A student breaks a lamp circuit and connects the voltmeter in line with the lamp rather than across it. What does the rest of the circuit do?

options.text: It behaves as an open circuit, so almost no current flows and the lamp stays dark
It behaves as a short circuit, so a very large current flows and the lamp glows
options.misconception: gives the voltmeter the near-zero resistance that belongs to an ammeter

options.text: It behaves as an open circuit, but the current keeps its normal working value
options.misconception: accepts the open circuit yet insists the current is unaffected by it

options.text: It behaves as a short circuit, and the lamp glows at its normal brightness
options.misconception: gives the voltmeter the wrong resistance and an impossible brightness

questions.explanation: A near-infinite resistance in series leaves no current for anything else, so the branch current collapses to almost nothing and the lamp goes dark while the voltmeter itself now shows nearly the whole supply voltage. Calling this a short circuit swaps the two instruments: a short is a near-zero resistance in series, which is the fault an ammeter placement can cause, not a voltmeter placement. An open circuit cannot leave the current at its normal value, because the current is what the open removes.
questions.hint: Compare the resistance the voltmeter brings with the resistance of the lamp beside it.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Diode direction of conduction
questions.learningObjective: state which way a diode conducts and what voltage it drops
questions.stem: A silicon diode sits in a circuit with its anode held at a potential 0.70 V above its cathode. What does the diode do at that bias?

options.text: It conducts, and nearly all the applied voltage falls across the diode itself
It blocks, because a diode can only conduct in the reverse direction
options.misconception: reverses the direction of conduction, which is the whole point of a diode

options.text: It conducts, and almost none of the applied voltage falls across the diode
options.misconception: expects an ideal zero-drop diode and misses the 0.70 V threshold

options.text: It conducts both ways round, dropping 0.70 V whichever way it is biased
options.misconception: believes the 0.70 V is a symmetric drop rather than a forward threshold

questions.explanation: A diode conducts when its anode is made positive relative to its cathode, and a silicon one needs about 0.70 V of forward bias before it passes current appreciably, so at that bias it conducts and the 0.70 V appears across it. The blocking case is the opposite bias, where essentially nothing passes, and that asymmetry is what lets a diode steer current one way round a circuit. The symmetric answer erases the behaviour that gives diodes their use, and the zero-drop answer is the idealisation that real silicon does not obey.
questions.hint: Ask which terminal has to be held positive for the diode to pass current.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Bridge rectifier
questions.learningObjective: state what a bridge rectifier does to an alternating supply
questions.stem: The secondary of a transformer delivers an alternating voltage that reverses sign on every half cycle. What does a bridge rectifier built from four diodes hand on to the circuit that follows?

options.text: A full-wave pulsating direct current, pulsing at twice the supply frequency
A steady direct current with no ripple, because the bridge smooths the wave
options.misconception: expects rectification alone to remove the ripple, which needs a reservoir

options.text: An alternating current at twice the supply frequency, switched up by the diodes
options.misconception: believes the diodes speed the supply up instead of reversing its pulses

options.text: A half-wave pulsating direct current, using only one diode of the four
options.misconception: describes a single-diode half-wave rectifier rather than the full bridge

questions.explanation: The four diodes are wired so that whichever way the secondary voltage points, one diagonal pair conducts and the load current always runs the same way, so every half cycle delivers a pulse of the same polarity and the pulse rate doubles. That gives a unidirectional but still rippling supply. Turning that ripple into a flat line is the job of a smoothing capacitor and the load resistance, not of the bridge, which is why the no-ripple answer is wrong.
questions.hint: Count how many half cycles reach the load and check the polarity of each.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: What a potentiometer wiper does
questions.learningObjective: describe the role of the wiper in a potentiometer
questions.stem: A potentiometer is wired across a supply with its wiper left connected to nothing else. What does moving the wiper along the track change?

options.text: The fraction of the supply voltage available between the wiper and one end
The total resistance of the track, and so the current drawn from the supply
options.misconception: believes the wiper changes the resistance in the supply path

options.text: The potential difference across the whole track, which the wiper can raise
options.misconception: believes the wiper can raise the supply voltage across the track

options.text: The current through the wiper contact, set by how firmly it is pressed
options.misconception: treats the wiper as a variable current sink rather than a tap

questions.explanation: The track is a uniform resistor across the supply, so the fraction of the track between the wiper and one end sets the fraction of the supply voltage the wiper can deliver, and that is how a potentiometer works as a volume control or a sensor input. The current drawn from the supply is set by the whole track and does not change. If something is connected to the wiper, as it always is in practice, it loads the tap and pulls the voltage away from the ideal fraction.
questions.hint: Ask what fraction of the track lies between the wiper and one end.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Thermistor as a temperature sensor
questions.learningObjective: infer the sign of a thermistor's temperature coefficient from a divider reading
questions.stem: A fixed resistor and a thermistor form a potential divider across a 5.0 V supply, and the output is measured across the thermistor. As the temperature rises the output voltage falls. What does that show about the thermistor?

options.text: Its resistance falls as the temperature rises
Its resistance rises as the temperature rises
options.misconception: reads the falling output as rising resistance, missing which arm the reading is across

options.text: The fixed resistor's resistance rises as the temperature rises
options.misconception: blames the fixed arm, which is the one held at constant resistance

options.text: The supply voltage falls as the temperature rises
options.misconception: blames the source instead of the divider ratio

questions.explanation: The output is taken across the thermistor, so when the output falls while the supply stays put, the thermistor is taking a smaller share of the total resistance, and its resistance has fallen. This is the behaviour of the common negative temperature coefficient type, which is why thermistors are used in that divider to turn temperature into a voltage a circuit can read. Blaming the fixed resistor fails because it is a plain resistor, and blaming the supply fails because the supply is a separate, regulated part of the circuit.
questions.hint: Fix the supply voltage and ask which arm lost resistance when the reading fell.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Light-dependent resistor as a sensor
questions.learningObjective: infer how a light-dependent resistor's resistance responds to brightness
questions.stem: A fixed resistor and a light-dependent resistor form a potential divider across a supply, with the output taken across the light-dependent resistor. In brighter light the output voltage falls. What does that show?

options.text: The light-dependent resistor's resistance falls as the light gets brighter
The light-dependent resistor's resistance rises as the light gets brighter
options.misconception: reads the falling output as rising resistance in the measured arm

options.text: The fixed resistor's resistance falls as the light gets brighter
options.misconception: blames the arm whose resistance is not light dependent

options.text: The output falls because more current is drawn from the supply
options.misconception: blames a current change rather than the divider ratio

questions.explanation: The supply is unchanged and the output is measured across the light-dependent resistor, so a lower reading means that arm now makes up a smaller share of the total resistance, which means its resistance has fallen. Carriers released by stronger illumination are exactly why: more light means more charge carriers available, so the material conducts better. The fixed resistor is ordinary and does not respond to light, and the total current through the divider does fall, but that is a consequence of the arm's resistance falling, not the cause of the reading.
questions.hint: The supply is constant, so a lower output can only mean a smaller share of the resistance.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Capacitor in a direct current circuit
questions.learningObjective: predict the steady-state behaviour of a capacitor in a direct current circuit
questions.stem: A capacitor and a resistor are in series across a direct current supply, and the switch has been closed for a long time. What current is flowing in that branch by then?

options.text: Essentially zero, because a charged capacitor blocks any further steady current
The same as at the instant of closing, because a current never changes
options.misconception: believes the charging current persists for as long as the switch is shut

options.text: The same as through the resistor alone, because the capacitor is now a wire
options.misconception: believes a charged capacitor conducts like plain conducting wire

options.text: Halved, because the charge on the capacitor leaks away at a steady rate
options.misconception: invents a steady leakage current through a charged capacitor

questions.explanation: A steady current would keep adding charge to a plate that is already at the supply potential, so as the capacitor charges, its own voltage climbs until it matches the supply and no further current can flow. What is left is a very small leakage current, so essentially zero. The initial current is the largest, set by the resistance alone, and it decays over a time set by the product of resistance and capacitance, which is why the lamp in such a circuit flashes and then goes dark.
questions.hint: Ask whether charge can keep arriving once the capacitor voltage equals the supply.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Maximum power transfer condition
questions.learningObjective: state the load resistance that takes greatest power from a source with internal resistance
questions.stem: A cell of emf 12.0 V and internal resistance 2.0 ohms drives a variable load resistor. Which value of load resistance takes the greatest power from the cell?

options.text: 2.0 ohms, matching the internal resistance of the cell
0 ohms, shorting the cell so that the largest current flows
options.misconception: optimises the current alone and forgets the voltage collapses to nothing

options.text: 12.0 ohms, using the emf of the cell expressed in ohms
options.misconception: reads a voltage in volts as if it were a resistance in ohms

options.text: A very large resistance, so that almost no current is drawn at all
options.misconception: optimises the voltage alone and forgets the current has collapsed to nothing

questions.explanation: Power is current times voltage, and both factors move the wrong way as the load is made smaller: the current rises but the voltage left for the load falls faster, and at a short circuit the load power is exactly zero, while at an open circuit the current is zero and so is the power. The product peaks when the load resistance equals the internal resistance, where the terminal voltage is half the emf and half the total power reaches the load. The trick answers each take one factor to an extreme and drop the other.
questions.hint: Both current and terminal voltage change as you vary the load, so examine the product.

questions.topic: Current in a series loop
questions.learningObjective: compute the current in a single loop of series resistors
questions.stem: A 24.0 V ideal supply drives a single loop containing resistors of 4.0 ohms, 8.0 ohms, and 12.0 ohms in series. What current circulates in the loop, in amperes? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: One path means the same current crosses each resistor, so the potential drops add and so do the resistances: 4.0 plus 8.0 plus 12.0 gives 24.0 ohms, and 24.0 V over 24.0 ohms is 1.00 A. A back-substitution closes it: 1.00 A through each resistor gives drops of 4.0, 8.0 and 12.0 V, which add back to the 24.0 V of the supply. Adding the reciprocals instead would be the parallel rule, and there is only one path here.
questions.hint: One path means one current, so the drops add and so do the resistances.

questions.topic: Time constant from a charging table
questions.learningObjective: extract a time constant from logged charging currents
questions.stem: A capacitor charges through a resistor from a 5.0 V supply, and the current is logged as 0.200 A at 0.0 s, 0.0736 A at 5.0 s, and 0.0271 A at 10.0 s. What time constant does that sequence give?

2.5 seconds, because the current has fallen to about 0.37 of its start
options.misconception: reads the same 0.37 ratio but sets the time constant at half the interval

options.text: 10.0 seconds, because the current has fallen to about 0.14 of its start
options.misconception: takes the elapsed time as the time constant rather than the fall factor

options.text: 5.0 seconds, because the current has fallen to half of its start
options.misconception: gives the right value with a decay factor that describes a different circuit

questions.explanation: The charging current falls by a factor of 0.368 for every time constant, and 0.0736 over 0.200 is 0.368, so 5.0 s is one time constant. options.misconception: denies that the resistance changes, which is exactly what heating does

options.misconception: leaves the current or voltage unsquared, so the units are not watts

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Where the energy goes when an inductive circuit is broken
questions.learningObjective: explain the spark at the contacts of a switch breaking an inductive circuit
questions.stem: A large coil is wired in series with a lamp and a supply, and once the switch has been shut the circuit carries a steady current. The moment the switch is opened the contacts glow with a small bright spark. Explain in your own words where that energy comes from and why the coil makes it happen.

answer.exemplar: The coil has been storing energy in its magnetic field, equal to half its inductance times the square of the current, and as long as the current flows that energy is held there. Opening the switch asks the current to stop instantly, and the coil refuses: its induced voltage jumps to whatever value is needed to keep the current flowing, and with nowhere else for it to go that voltage appears across the widening gap between the contacts. Once the gap voltage is high enough it ionises the air and the current continues through the spark, dumping the field energy as heat and light. A plain lamp circuit has nothing to push back, so the current simply stops at the gap with no spark at all.

questions.explanation: This is the practical face of self-induction: the coil cannot let its current change suddenly, so breaking the circuit forces a high voltage across the break, and that voltage is what lights the gap. The energy is not created at the contacts; it is the field energy that was already stored, released all at once. Asking why the spark is bright is the same question as asking where the field energy went, and the answer is that it became heat, light, and a puff of metal vapour.
questions.hint: Ask what the coil was storing while the current flowed, and where that must go.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: The drop across a cell's internal resistance
questions.learningObjective: explain why a loaded cell reads below its labelled emf
questions.stem: A cell is labelled 12.0 V, yet a voltmeter across its terminals reads 11.4 V while a lamp drawing 5.0 A is connected. Explain in your own words what the missing 0.6 V means and where it is being used up.

answer.exemplar: The label gives the emf, the voltage the cell would supply if nothing at all were drawn from it. The instant current leaves, some of that emf is dropped across the cell's own internal resistance, here 0.12 ohms, since 0.6 V at 5.0 A needs 0.12 ohms, and that leaves 11.4 V at the terminals. The power being lost is I squared times r, which here is 3.0 W, and it becomes heat inside the cell. This is why a cell warms up when it is working hard and why the reading climbs back towards 12.0 V the moment the lamp is switched off.

questions.explanation: The gap between the label and the measurement is not an instrument error: it is the internal resistance, and the power lost in it grows as the square of the current, so a heavily loaded cell both reads low and gets hot. Working backwards from the two readings gives the internal resistance directly, and that figure is the one that predicts the behaviour at any other load.
questions.hint: Find the current, divide the missing volts by it, and consider where I squared r goes.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Why a capacitor branch stops conducting direct current
questions.learningObjective: explain the transient and steady-state behaviour of a charging capacitor
questions.stem: A capacitor is in series with a lamp and a direct current supply. The lamp flashes brightly just after the switch closes, but a few seconds later it is dark even though the switch is still shut. Explain in your own words what has changed in that branch.

answer.exemplar: At the instant of closing, the plates of the capacitor carry no charge, so there is no voltage across it and it offers almost no opposition, and the current is limited only by the lamp, which is why the flash is at full brightness. As that current flows, charge builds on the plates and a voltage appears across the capacitor that opposes the supply. Once that voltage has climbed to the supply voltage no further charge can be pushed in, the current stops, and the lamp goes dark. How long the flash lasts is set by the product of the resistance and the capacitance, the time constant, so a bigger capacitor or a bigger resistor stretches the visible flash out.

questions.explanation: The capacitor does not consume current; it fills up. Because charge and a voltage have to accumulate before the branch current can die away, the behaviour is time-dependent rather than instantaneous, and the time constant is the single number that sets the whole shape. Charging a large capacitor through a small resistance is a common way of making a short sharp flash, and through a large resistance of making a long soft one.
questions.hint: Track the voltage across the capacitor, not the charge on the plates.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Why maximum power transfer needs a matched load
questions.learningObjective: explain why the greatest load power needs the load to match the internal resistance
questions.stem: Someone argues that a cell should push the most power into a lamp when the lamp's resistance is made as small as possible, because then the largest current flows. Explain in your own words why that reasoning fails, and what the load resistance has to be instead.

answer.exemplar: Power is the product of current and voltage, and the two factors move in opposite directions as the load is made smaller. Lower the load resistance and the current does rise, but more of the emf is dropped across the cell's own internal resistance, so the voltage left for the load falls faster than the current rises. In the limit of a perfect short the current is at its largest and the power in the load is exactly zero, because no voltage reaches it, and in the limit of an open circuit the current is zero and so is the power. The product therefore has a maximum in between, at a load resistance equal to the internal resistance, where the load gets half the emf and half the total power while the cell wastes the other half as heat.

questions.explanation: The argument fails because it holds one factor of the product fixed while the other moves, and both factors depend on the load. Maximum power transfer is a statement about the compromise between a high current and a high voltage, not a preference for either one on its own. It also explains why a cell that is shorted gets hot rather than useful, since in that case all the released power is being dissipated internally.
questions.hint: Write power as the product of the current and the voltage actually across the load.
